extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying introductory discrete mathematics / foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook chapter material covering the pigeonhole principle, function composition, inverse relations/functions, images/preimages, and cardinality — giving definitions, theorems, example applications, and exercises for learning and proof practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Pigeonhole Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A and B are finite sets and f : A -> B is any function. Then: 1. If |A| > |B|, then f is not injective. 2. If |A| < |B|, then f is not surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with figures: more pigeons than holes implies some pigeon-hole receives at least two pigeons (non-injective); fewer pigeons than holes implies at least one empty hole (non-surjective). Used in nonconstructive existence proofs; examples given include: (a) any set of 10 integers from 1..100 has two distinct subsets with equal sum (proof via mapping subsets to their sums and comparing cardinalities); (b) at least two Texans have the same number of hairs (map Texans to possible hair counts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-sum subsets in 10 integers (application of pigeonhole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition: If A is any set of 10 integers between 1 and 100, then there exist two different subsets X ⊂ A and Y ⊂ A for which the sum of elements in X equals the sum of elements in Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs f: P(A) -> {0,1,...,1000} sending a subset to its sum. Since |P(A)| = 2^10 = 1024 > 1001, pigeonhole principle implies f not injective, yielding two distinct subsets with equal sum. Examples illustrate specific sets and sums. Emphasizes nonconstructive nature of such proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole example: identical hair counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition: There are at least two Texans with the same number of hairs on their heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Let A be Texans and B = {0,1,2,...,1000000}. Population of Texas > 20,000,000 while maximum hair counts < 1,000,000, so |A| > |B|; define f(x) = number of hairs on x's head. By pigeonhole principle f is not injective, so two Texans share the same hair count. Note the proof is existence-only (nonconstructive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of functions (Definition 12.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A -> B and g : B -> C then the composition gof : A -> C is defined by (g o f)(x) = g(f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful with order: symbol gof means apply f first then g. Composition also makes sense if range(f) ⊆ domain(g) (not just when codomain equals domain). Examples show when composition is defined and when it's not (if codomain of f differs from domain of g). Remark: composition need not be commutative (g o f may differ from f o g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Associativity of composition (Theorem 12.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of functions is associative: if f : A -> B, g : B -> C, h : C -> D, then ((h o g) o f) = (h o (g o f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by evaluating both sides on an arbitrary x in A and noting both equal h(g(f(x))). Useful when composing multiple functions — parentheses can be omitted in expressions like h o g o f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity (Theorem 12.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A -> B and g : B -> C, then: (a) if both f and g are injective, g o f is injective; (b) if both f and g are surjective, g o f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches provided: for injectivity use g(f(x)) = g(f(y)) -> f(x)=f(y) (since g injective) -> x=y (since f injective). For surjectivity, given c in C find b with g(b)=c (g surjective) and a with f(a)=b (f surjective), then g(f(a))=c. The text emphasizes checking preimages/targets when showing surjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function (Definition 12.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a set A, the identity function i_A : A -> A is defined by i_A(x) = x for every x ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity functions are bijective (trivially injective and surjective). Examples: i_{ {1,2,3} } = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)}. Identities appear in identities for inverses: f^{-1} o f = i_A and f o f^{-1} = i_B when inverses exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation (Definition 12.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a relation R from A to B, the inverse relation R^{-1} is the relation from B to A defined by R^{-1} = { (y,x) : (x,y) ∈ R }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If R is a function, its inverse relation need not be a function (it may fail the functional property if original function is not injective, and may fail to be total if original not surjective). Examples show both cases: inverse of a bijection is a function, inverse of a non-injective or non-surjective function is not a function. Thus bijectivity is necessary and sufficient for the inverse relation to be a function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation is a function iff f is bijective (Theorem 12.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : A -> B be a function. Then f is bijective if and only if the inverse relation f^{-1} is a function from B to A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f is bijective then f^{-1} is a function and satisfies f^{-1}(f(x)) = x for all x ∈ A, so f^{-1} o f = i_A and f o f^{-1} = i_B. Conversely if f^{-1} is a function then f must be both injective and surjective. The theorem underpins when one can talk about 'the' inverse function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse function (Definition 12.8 and computational method)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A -> B is bijective then its inverse is the function f^{-1} : B -> A satisfying f^{-1} o f = i_A and f o f^{-1} = i_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard technique to compute inverses for bijective formulas: write y = f(x), interchange variables to x = f(y), then solve for y to obtain y = f^{-1}(x). Examples include algebraic inversion of polynomials and solving linear systems when f is a bijection on product sets (e.g., Z x Z). Always verify by checking compositions yield identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and preimage (Definition 12.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A -> B and X ⊆ A, the image f(X) = { f(x) : x ∈ X } ⊆ B. For Y ⊆ B the preimage f^{-1}(Y) = { x ∈ A : f(x) ∈ Y } ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes X and Y are subsets (not elements). Preimage f^{-1}(Y) is defined even if f not invertible. Examples demonstrate computing images and preimages, and subtle distinctions between f({a}) = {f(a)} and f(a) = value. Warns that f(f^{-1}(Y)) may be different from Y and f^{-1}(f(X)) may be larger than X in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic properties of images and preimages (Theorem 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes which inclusions can be strict (e.g., f(W ∩ X) may be a proper subset of f(W) ∩ f(X)); exercises ask for proofs and counterexamples. These identities are basic tools when reasoning about functions and sets, particularly in analysis and algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality equality via bijection (Definition 13.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets A and B have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|, if there exists a bijective function f : A -> B. If no such bijection exists, the sets have unequal cardinalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to both finite and infinite sets. Introduces bijection/injection/surjection terminology. Emphasizes that bijections identify sets as having equal 'size' (including infinite examples); equality of cardinality is an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive). Examples: explicit bijection between two finite sets or between N and Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijection N <-> Z (Theorem 13.1 / Example 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a bijection f : N -> Z, hence |N| = |Z|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example gives an explicit table/listing that pairs natural numbers with integers in alternating order (0,1,-1,2,-2,...). The text suggests producing a formula for that bijection. Demonstrates that infinite sets can have unintuitive equalities of cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's diagonal argument: |N| < |R| (Theorem 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists no bijection f : N -> R; therefore |N| ≠ |R| (indeed |N| < |R| in the usual sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagonal argument: write reals f(n) in decimal expansion, construct a real b whose nth decimal differs from the nth decimal of f(n) (e.g., make it 0 if f(n)'s digit ≠ 0, else 1). Then b ≠ f(n) for all n, so f not surjective. This shows there are strictly more reals than naturals. Text gives an informal description and a worked diagonal construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijections between intervals and rays (Examples 13.3 and 13.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples showing |(0,∞)| = |(0,1)| (via a geometric projection/bijection) and |R| = |(0,1)| (compose bijections R -> (0,∞) via g(x)=2^x and (0,∞) -> (0,1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric description: for (0,∞) to (0,1) map x to intersection of line from P = (-1,1) to (x,0) with y-axis, yielding f(x) = x/(x+1). Use transitivity of cardinality via composition of bijections. These examples illustrate techniques to produce explicit bijections between apparently different infinite sets.
